name: 粟 ならまち店 (Awa Naramachi-ten)

claims.text: Menu includes tempura (wheat-flour batter) and millet/grain-based wagashi, and Japanese seasoning relies on soy sauce and miso; no gluten-free handling or separate equipment is documented.
As a Japanese kaiseki-style kitchen the dishes use standard soy sauce and miso, which typically contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

The kitchen prepares Yamato beef and local chicken alongside the vegetable courses, and Japanese stocks generally use fish-based dashi; shared preparation and dashi are likely unless arranged in advance.

A dedicated vegetable course ('Yamato and World Vegetables', about ¥4,800) is offered, and the entire restaurant is built around vegetables, so vegetarian/vegan accommodation is plausible if requested when reserving.
Vegetables come from the restaurant's own pesticide-free farm near Nara, with seasonal heirloom varieties as the centerpiece of every course.

name: ベーカリーポポロ (Bakery Poporo)

claims.text: This is a conventional bakery producing wheat bread on the same premises and equipment as its rice flour breads, so airborne flour and shared-surface cross-contamination is highly likely; no dedicated gluten-free handling is documented.

Dairy and animal products (cream cheese, milk chocolate cream, butter, sausage, smoked chicken, salted mackerel) are used throughout the lineup, so vegan items, if any, would be prepared in a non-vegan environment.
A range of rice flour (komeko) breads is a regular part of the menu, offering a wheat-reduced option for those who are not strictly celiac.
Signature dishes are wheat-based pasta; no gluten-free menu or cross-contamination protocol is documented, so the kitchen handles wheat throughout.
An omnivore Italian kitchen using Yamato pork, cream and cheese; no documented separation for vegan diners, so cross-contact with dairy and meat should be assumed unless confirmed.
Heavy use of the restaurant's own organic Nara vegetables and a fully vegetable-based cafe-time shaved ice menu offers some plant-forward options.

name: ブーランジェリー リッシュ (Boulangerie Riche)

claims.text: An entirely flour-based bakery with no documented gluten-free area or products; airborne flour and shared surfaces make heavy cross-contamination unavoidable.

Dairy- and egg-containing doughs and fillings (milk bread, condensed-milk anpan, cheese focaccia, croissants) are made in the same kitchen, so any incidentally plant-based item would share equipment with animal products.

name: ブタとエスプレッソと (Buta to Espresso to)

claims.text: The kitchen deep-fries wheat-breaded pork cutlets (tonkatsu, katsu curry, katsudon) in a small space, making cross-contact with gluten very likely; no dedicated gluten-free preparation is documented.
The curry sauce itself is simmered with chicken stock (鶏ガラ) and the menu is entirely pork-centered, so there is no vegan-safe dish to begin with.

name: カフェ エトランジェ・ナラッド (Cafe Etranger Narad)

claims.text: The menu is built around Neapolitan pizza, pasta and bread, so wheat is widespread in the kitchen and cross-contamination is likely; no gluten-free handling is documented.

One listing for the signature tofu hamburger box states it can accommodate vegan, vegetarian and allergy requests and is additive-free, suggesting some willingness to adapt, but this is not detailed for the full menu and should be confirmed directly.
Cooking emphasizes local Yamato vegetables and offers a tofu-based hamburger box, giving vegetarian and plant-leaning diners a real anchor dish.

Menu relies on Japanese seasonings and dashi-flavored items (e.g., dashi-flavored Ōmi red konnyaku, sake-lees soup), implying standard wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free alternative is mentioned.
Vegetable-forward but not vegan: signature plates feature meat and fish/dashi sides, with no documented separation for plant-based diners.

Everything from the pre-meal vinegar to soups and dressings is made in-house and the kitchen uses no chemical seasonings, so ingredients are largely from scratch — helpful for asking about specific items.

The entire menu is wheat-free and gluten-free, so there is no wheat flour in the kitchen to cross-contaminate; sweets use the owner's homemade rice flour. No formal celiac protocol or dedicated-fryer statement is published, so confirm seasonings directly if you are highly sensitive.

Miso soup uses homemade miso and a vegetable-based (non-fish) stock; the site does not specify whether any soy sauce used is wheat-free tamari, so celiac diners should ask about soy sauce / miso ingredients.
The whole kitchen is plant-based (no meat, fish, dairy, or egg on the menu), so animal cross-contact risk is minimal.
The owner offers to flexibly accommodate requests if consulted in advance, suggesting individual dietary questions can be discussed before visiting.

Every item on the menu is both vegan and gluten-free, made with home-grown vegetables and homemade rice flour and miso, making it one of the safest single-stop choices in central Nara for travelers needing both diets.
